newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran's new president mandated to bring change.
newsitem.headline: Iran's new president mandated to bring change.

text.p: Mohammad Khatami comes to the Iranian presidency with an electoral mandate for change that will be quickly tested in the trade-offs inherent in the Islamic republic's factional political system.
Diplomats and Iran-watchers expect the first months of Khatami's four-year administration, starting next week, to be crucial in setting its tone and reforming scope.
His ability to steer his own supporters into cabinet positions after screening by a combative parliament will be watched particularly closely.

Khatami's landslide election victory in May was largely delivered by ranks of discontented youth, the middle classes and women who rallied to the 54-year-old Shi'ite Moslem cleric's espousal of a civil society within the context of the Islamic republic, the rule of law and more social and cultural freedoms.
"The call for change and for a more pluralist society from voters could not have been clearer. The proud nationalism remains but daily life has to be made easier," said a diplomat in Tehran.

Khatami won nearly 70 percent of the ballot, or 20 million votes, based on a programme "to accept pluralism and variety of views within our system and laws". He is due to take the oath of office on Monday.
He was known as an educated, moderate cleric during a previous stint in office as culture minister which relaxed press freedoms and introduced less stringent social restrictions.
Eighteen years of revolution, encompassing an eight-year war with Iraq and increasing U.S. trade sanctions, brought a major change in sentiment by the time voters went to the polls.

Khatami faced a difficult balancing act to meet voters' expectations while reaching consensus with a conservative parliament led by his defeated campaign rival, speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, diplomats said.
"A critical juncture is to observe how far Khatami can follow his own path and how much he will use his election majority to press for change," said a Tehran-based diplomat.
Conservative Moslem clerics have already put pressure on Khatami over his choice of ministers, Iran newspapers report.
"The Majlis won't miss an opportunity to shape a cabinet as close as possible to its own complexion...Trade-offs are inevitable," a European embassy source said.

Khatami has said he will look across factional lines in his cabinet appointees though analysts predict he would be unlikely to give ground on the key posts of interior, intelligence, foreign affairs, culture and finance.
Contests between Khatami and the Majlis go on behind the uncontested authority of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, heir to the revolution's founder Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.
Khamenei also controls foreign policy, particularly concerning relations with Iran's arch-foes America and Israel.

The political landscape is complicated further by the appointment of outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani to head the Expediency Council, where he will remain a major force drawing up long-term policies and advising Khamenei.
The support of pro-Rafsanjani officials, often tagged moderate reformers, was crucial in Khatami's election victory.
Rafsanjani has already been reported to back the creation of political parties in Iran. These were banned after 1979.

"The big question is whether the Islamic republic in its present form has the ability to accommodate the heightened expectations of the electorate...Khatami has popular support but no guarantee of success to carry out deep reform," said one Western diplomatic source in the country.

Any quick reforms of the status of women -- advocated by Khatami during his election campaign -- are unlikely as the new president is expected to be pressured by many state bodies controlled by the conservatives.
The naming of a woman to Khatami's cabinet, the first female appointment since 1979, is expected.

Though diplomats expect little from Khatami in the first months of office his presidency offers the best chance for a change in Tehran-Washington hostility and an improved relationship with the European Union.
EU ambassadors were withdrawn from Tehran after a German court ruled in April that Iran's top leaders had ordered political assassinations of dissidents in Berlin in 1992.
Economic policy is not expected to undergo major changes in Khatami's first months in office as he inherits a five-year, centrally-planned, economic plan that runs to the year 2000.

The need to bring down inflation, officially running at just short of 20 percent, to create jobs through stimulating the non-oil sector and ensure that the country's foreign debt does not return to unmanageable levels will be prime goals.
